title: Effective generators of the Picard group of a flag variety
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Group schemes and their homomorphisms are as in [def-sc-group-scheme]. All algebraic groups in this statement are affine and of finite type over $F$ [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Smoothness and connectedness are as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. For an $F$-scheme $X$, $\operatorname{Pic}(X)$ denotes the abelian group of isomorphism classes of invertible $\mathcal O_X$-modules, with tensor product as addition and zero the class of $\mathcal O_X$; an invertible module is one Zariski locally isomorphic to $\mathcal O_X$. A Borel subgroup of a smooth connected group $G$ is a maximal smooth connected solvable closed subgroup; solvable means that iterating the derived subgroup eventually gives the trivial group, and the derived subgroup is the smallest closed subgroup through which the commutator morphism factors. Let $G$ be smooth connected and $B\subseteq G$ a Borel subgroup. The quotient $Q=G/B$ means the $F$-scheme representing the fppf sheafification of $A\mapsto G(A)/B(A)$ on commutative $F$-algebras; here fppf coverings are jointly surjective faithfully flat finitely presented coverings. Write $\pi:G\to Q$ for the quotient morphism. There is an integer $r\geq0$ and invertible modules $\mathcal L_1,\ldots,\mathcal L_r$ on $Q$ whose classes generate $\operatorname{Pic}(Q)$ as an abelian group, with $\Gamma(Q,\mathcal L_i)\ne0$ for every $i$. Generation means that every class is an integer linear combination of these classes; $r=0$ is allowed.

source.place: Lemma 18.21 and its proof, printed p.392: divisor classes supported on the boundary of the affine-space cell, using Proposition 13.52 and the proof of Theorem 17.65.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-borel-quotient-affine-cell] to the given $G$ and $B$. It gives a regular integral Noetherian separated scheme $Q$ and a dense open $U\simeq\mathbf A_F^n$. These are exactly the hypotheses needed below for rational sections and divisors on $Q$. In particular $U$ contains the generic point of $Q$.

source.place: Lemma 18.21, first two sentences of the proof, p.392; Proposition 13.52 and proof of Theorem 17.65.

proof.text: The closed subset $Z=|Q|\setminus|U|$ has finitely many irreducible components by [lem-sc-noetherian-closed-subset-finite-components]. Select those of codimension one and give them their reduced closed subscheme structures; write them $E_1,\ldots,E_r$. These are precisely all prime divisors of $Q$ contained in $Z$: any such prime divisor $D_0$ lies in a component $W$ of $Z$, and strict containment in $W$ would give the chain $D_0\subsetneq W\subsetneq Q$ of irreducible closed subsets, contradicting codimension one. Thus $r$ is finite, possibly zero.

source.place: Lemma 18.21, final two sentences of the proof: finite boundary and its codimension-one components.

proof.text: Each $E_i$ is an effective Cartier divisor. Indeed, at $x\in E_i$ its ideal in $A=\mathcal O_{Q,x}$ is the height-one prime corresponding to its generic point. Regularity makes $A$ a UFD by [lem-trf-regular-local-ufd-boundary-factorization], applied with the empty list of parameters. The height-one criterion [lem-trf-ufd-height-one] makes this ideal $(f)$ with $f\ne0$; since $A$ is a domain, $f$ is a nonzerodivisor. Outside $E_i$ its ideal is generated by $1$. The scheme clause of [lem-sfb-stalk-nonzerodivisor-cartier-spreading] now supplies effective Cartier local equations on an open cover. This is the argument of Stacks 0AGA, not an assertion that a global equation exists.

For each $i$ take $\mathcal L_i=\mathcal O_Q(E_i)$ from [lem-sfb-regular-space-divisor-line-dictionary]. It is invertible. Its canonical rational section $1$ is regular: on a chart with effective Cartier equation $f$, the module is $f^{-1}\mathcal O_Q$, and $1=f\cdot f^{-1}$ belongs to it. These local sections agree in the rational-function sheaf, hence glue globally. On $U$, $f$ is a unit and this section is a generator, so it is nonzero. Consequently $\Gamma(Q,\mathcal L_i)\ne0$.

source.place: Tag 0AGA and the local inverse-equation construction; Tag 01WX, definition-invertible-sheaf-effective-Cartier-divisor, canonical section.

proof.text: Let $M$ be any invertible module on $Q$. By [lem-sfb-affine-space-invertible-trivial], $M|_U\simeq\mathcal O_U$; take the section corresponding to $1$. Its generic value defines a nonzero rational section $s$ of $M$. By [lem-sfb-regular-space-divisor-line-dictionary], $D=\operatorname{div}(s)$ is a finite Weil divisor, $M\simeq\mathcal O_Q(D)$, and divisor formation respects restriction. Since $s|_U$ is everywhere generating, its divisor on $U$ is zero. Thus every prime divisor with nonzero coefficient in $D$ lies in $Z$, and step 2 gives $D=\sum_{i=1}^r a_iE_i$ for integers $a_i$.

source.place: Lemma 18.21, proof, p.392: Picard triviality on the affine-space cell and boundary-supported divisor representatives.

proof.text: The local description in [lem-sfb-regular-space-divisor-line-dictionary] identifies $\mathcal O_Q(\sum_i a_iE_i)$ with $\bigotimes_i\mathcal O_Q(E_i)^{\otimes a_i}$. Explicitly choose simultaneous local equations $f_i$ for the finitely many $E_i$; both sides are the free rank-one fractional module $(\prod_i f_i^{a_i})^{-1}\mathcal O_Q$. Multiplication gives the isomorphisms and they agree on overlaps as maps inside the rational-function field. Negative exponents use the dual line. Step 5 therefore gives $[M]=\sum_i a_i[\mathcal L_i]$. If $r=0$, the same calculation has empty product $1$ and shows every $M$ trivial. Together with step 4 this proves both required clauses.

source.place: Local inverse-equation construction for Cartier divisors, as in Tag 01WX; Milne Lemma 18.21, conclusion.
